args.text: [lane-ibis] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System, the internet's address book) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: if a site moves to a new server, users keep being sent to the old one, so it may appear down. (2) Slow recovery from faults or attacks: a wrong or poisoned answer stays stored for longer, so harm lasts after the fix. (3) Hampered failover and migration: switching traffic to a backup server takes longer, because many resolvers keep using the old answer until it expires.

[lane-ibis] An idempotent action gives the same result however many times it is run, so repeating it after a timeout or failure does no extra harm. This matters because a sender often cannot tell whether the first attempt worked, and safe retries avoid problems such as charging a customer twice or creating duplicate records.

[lane-ibis] Two trade-offs of UUIDv7 as a primary key. (1) It leaks creation time, because the first part of the ID is a millisecond timestamp, so outsiders can estimate when a record was made. (2) It is 16 bytes, larger than a 4 or 8 byte integer, so indexes use more space, and IDs made in the same millisecond on different servers are only roughly ordered.

[lane-ibis] A write-ahead log (WAL) is a file where a database records each change before applying it to the main data, so the change is safely stored first. After a crash, the database replays this log to recover completed changes and undo unfinished ones, which keeps data consistent and durable.

[lane-ibis] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Results stay comparable, because a newer client may change defaults, retries or connection handling and shift the numbers for reasons unrelated to the system under test. (2) Runs can be reproduced later, since anyone can rebuild the same setup and check the figures.

[lane-ibis] Backpressure is a way for a queue to signal producers to slow down or stop when consumers cannot keep up, instead of letting the queue grow without limit. It protects memory and latency by making the sender wait, drop work or retry later, so the whole system stays stable under load.

[lane-ibis] Two ways a cron job (a scheduled task) can run twice: (1) the same schedule is installed on two servers, for example after a failover or a copy of the config; (2) a slow run is still going when the next one starts, so the runs overlap. One guard: take a lock before starting, such as a lock file or a database lock, and exit at once if another run already holds it.

[lane-ibis] A tombstone is a marker written in place of a deleted record in a replicated store. It tells every copy that the data was deleted on purpose, so a replica that missed the delete does not bring the old value back. Tombstones are kept for a set time, then cleaned up once all copies have seen them.

[lane-ibis] Two signs a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no change between runs. (2) It fails only under certain conditions, such as a slow machine, a different run order, or a particular time, and passes when run again alone.

[lane-ibis] A lease lock gives a holder the lock until a set time. Clock skew means machines disagree about the time. A holder whose clock runs slow may think its lease is still valid after the lock service has expired it and given it to someone else. Then two holders act at once, which breaks the lock.
